Climbing isn’t hard. Carl is pulling. 🧗

Most beginners climb on their arms. Bent elbows, hips away from the wall, feet just along for the ride. Your forearms are toast in 30 seconds.

Try this on your next move:
1. Feet first – place your foot before you reach
2. Set the hips – get them over that foot, arms long
3. Then move – let your legs stand you up

Position first. Move second.

Save this and try it on your next session. Are you a Carl? ↓

Carl aimed perfectly. That was the problem.

Throw yourself straight at the hold and gravity bends your path below it. Carl missed by 65 cm.

The fix:
1. Pull your hips in to the wall.
2. Let your legs push you up, not out.
3. Aim the top of your arc at the hold. That’s the dead point: for a split second you’re weightless, and that’s when you grab.

Same wall, same hold. Carl sticks it.

On an overhang, hips that hang away from the wall let gravity pull your body into a sag. Your feet lose pressure and cut loose.

The fix: arms straight, hips in, core tight. Now the tension runs from your hands to your feet, and your feet stay on.

top.pie_completo:
A climbing career is a collection of moments.

We spend our days playing on rocks with friends, learning our craft, and seeing what we’re capable of. We find flow, rise to the occasion, and fall off the same move(s) more times than we’d like to admit 😝 Through all of that, we grow; sometimes in ways we can measure, and sometimes in ways we only recognize years later.

When I look back, each day seems to settle into one or two moments; a time I surprised myself, a friend cheering when I needed it (you know who you are), a failure I handled better than I would have before (the same people know this 🤣) . None necessarily more valuable than the others, but some stay with us longer.

Doing this dyno, (“Zeus,” V11/8A) on my first try, in front of a group of friends I’d just spent an unforgettable month with, will always be one of those moments. I remember the anticipation, the people watching, and the feeling of sharing something we all understood mattered. So much of what made it special happened in the weeks before I ever left the ground.

That’s why I keep training, learning, and trying so hard to improve; because getting better expands the experiences available to me (the climbs I can try, the places I can explore, and the occasions I feel ready to meet). Coaching lets me help other people create those possibilities for themselves.

The excitement of a big send can be surprisingly brief… You work toward something for months, do it, celebrate, and soon your mind starts searching for what comes next. It’s easy to mistake that fading excitement for evidence that the achievement didn’t mean much, but I can return to this memory, watch the video, remember those friends, and feel fulfilled all over again. The moment ended, but it’s value keeps unfolding.

If you’re questioning whether your effort is worth it, look beyond how you felt immediately after succeeding or failing. Think about what those experiences mean to you now; what do you treasure about your best days? What have your hardest days taught you and what would you change because of them?

What’s your favorite moment of your climbing career thus far?

#climbing #bouldering

Inside Flag: Episode 2 of “Elite Technique,” the series for climbers who want hard moves to feel suspiciously easy and their beta to look top notch.

The inside flag has been accused of bad technique. Today, we clear its name.

Also known as a “through flag,” “Can-Can,” or “Ferret Launcher” (a term I have courageously fabricated), it can help you oppose rotation and stay stable while reaching. Because ideally, only the hand you’re moving should leave the wall.

When your other leg(s) obstruct a backflag, or you need more opposition to the rotation around the hand you’re pulling from, an inside flag can be the better tool. Sometimes the answer is simply putting a leg somewhere deeply unintuitive.

However, it can also get you into a position that feels brilliant until you need to do literally anything else. Unwinding may then require a degree in human origami, and failure to graduate can result in an unscheduled departure from the climbing surface.

top.pie_completo:
Weirdest Climbing Technique Ever? The Lemay… 

Ep. 1 of “Elite Technique,” my new series for climbers who want to make hard moves feel easy and look suave AF doing it.

The Lemay is a sneaky lil thang. A technique lost to time, you could say…

Often called a “back” or “reverse” toehook/heelhook, a Lemay can serve similar functions to both.

The Lemay lets you leverage holds that FACE YOU or the direction you’re trying to move toward, whereas heelhooks and toehooks typically use holds that face away from you.

I’ll never forget watching someone use one to get through a sequence I’d set and thought only had one solution… lucas_oddi proved me wrong and introduced me to this move 10 years ago (and I’d already been climbing for 10 years and up to V12)!

Since then, it’s probably been my easiest way through 500–1,000 moves. Initially, the position felt awkward and my hip flexors felt weak because I’d never really pulled with my leg like that before.

But quality reps, focus, baby oil, and time helped me polish this method of keeping my hips close to the wall and adding pulling force to moves!

If you want to learn it, I’d recommend spending 15 minutes at the beginning of 1–2 sessions each week exploring where it works and finding easy versions. Repeat those until they feel like second nature, then make them harder and repeat the process.

Over time, you’ll start spotting more and more opportunities to use them on the climbs you naturally choose.

🚨 STOP THE OPEN DOOR! 5 WAYS TO FIX IT! 🟢

Ever had your foot suddenly pop off the wall when reaching for the next hold?

That's the open door effect!

When you reach outside your foot support, your body may start to rotate. On big footholds, you might not even notice it. But on smaller footholds or steep overhangs, it can become a real problem.

🟢 5 ways to control it:

1️⃣ Switch feet – create a stable triangle. 2️⃣ Backflag – control unwanted rotation. 3️⃣ Inside flag – extend your counterbalance. 4️⃣ Heel hook – create tension through your heel. 5️⃣ Toe hook – stabilize your body and control rotation.

The key isn't just knowing these techniques. It's understanding WHEN and WHY to use them.

That's exactly what structured climbing is about.

I specialize in teaching efficient climbing movement, especially on steep overhangs – from fundamental body positioning to advanced techniques.

¿De qué equipo eres? Dilo en comentarios y etiqueta al de tu grupo que siempre se queja de la altura.

From neil.gresham who developed his Masterclass Series years ahead of their time, to c4hp who’s consistently challenged the status quo of training approach to useful.coach who has some of the most thoughtful and nuanced nutrition advice out there. top.pie: ¿Los altos lo tienen más fácil? La altura en escalada importa menos de lo que crees 🧗 Un estudio con 44 escaladores encontró que la altura, el peso y la enverg
top.pie_completo:
¿Los altos lo tienen más fácil? La altura en escalada importa menos de lo que crees 🧗
Un estudio con 44 escaladores encontró que la altura, el peso y la envergadura casi no explicaban su nivel: un 0,3 %. Lo que más pesaba era lo que se entrena: un 58,9 %.
Y en un paso largo, lo que se entrena es girar la cadera: gira el pie sobre la punta hasta el canto de fuera, pega a la pared la cadera de la mano que sube, y entonces alarga.
¿Cuál es el paso que nunca te llega? 👇
Mándaselo al más alto de tu grupo.

📚 Fuentes
· Mermier, Janot, Parker y Swan (2000). Physiological and anthropometric determinants of sport climbing performance. British Journal of Sports Medicine 34: 359-365.
· REI: Climbing Techniques and Moves.
· Eric Hörst: Using the Twist-Lock to Optimize COG on Steep Terrain.
· Send Edition: Hip Turns in Climbing.
Es un estudio de 44 escaladores que mide el nivel general, no un paso concreto: en algunos pasos la altura sí ayuda.
